content:
The argument goes back to John of Damascus. Muslims say that the Quran is the eternal, uncreated Word of God. Christians say the same of the Word in John 1:1.

So, the argument runs, Islam has its own eternal Word beside God, and it should accept the Christian one. Harry Wolfson named the Muslim idea "inlibration", the Word made book, to set it beside incarnation.[1]

The six answers set out the history and the theology, and they show where the comparison breaks.

John of Damascus, writing in the eighth century, argued that the Quran calls Christ the Word and a Spirit from God (4:171). If God's Word is uncreated, he said, Muslims who call Christ a creature cut God off from His own Word.[2]

In 218 AH (833) the caliph al-Ma'mun required judges and scholars to affirm that the Quran is created. Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused and was flogged under al-Mu'tasim. Al-Mutawakkil ended the policy in about 234 to 237 AH (848 to 851).[3]

Wolfson argued that Christian teaching on the Logos shaped the debate. Wilferd Madelung traced the controversy to developments inside Muslim theology and doubted direct borrowing.[1][4]

For al-Ash'ari and al-Maturidi, God's speech (kalām nafsī) is an eternal attribute of God. The recited sounds, the ink and the pages are created.[5]

The classical formula says that God's attributes are "neither He nor other than He". An attribute has no separate existence. It is never worshipped, prayed to or embodied in a man.[5]

The Quran is recited and obeyed, and no Muslim prays to it. Surah 112 rules out any begetting in God.[6]

The Christian Logos is a person who becomes flesh (John 1:14). The analogy breaks at that point.

The Muslim answer keeps the Creator and the creature apart: the eternal speech belongs to God, and every copy and every recitation belongs to creation.

The comparison starts from a real likeness and ends at the doctrine of incarnation, which Islam rejects. The related articles are God's hand, face and throne in the Quran and 5 reasons why Muslims believe that Jesus is not God. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Harry A. Wolfson, The Philosophy of the Kalam (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1976), chapter 3.
  2. John of Damascus, De haeresibus 100, in Daniel J. Sahas, John of Damascus on Islam (Leiden: Brill, 1972); Quran 4:171.
  3. M. Hinds, "Miḥna", Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill), vol. 7.
  4. Wilferd Madelung, "The Origins of the Controversy Concerning the Creation of the Koran" (1974), reprinted in Religious Schools and Sects in Medieval Islam (London: Variorum, 1985).
  5. L. Gardet, "'Ilm al-Kalām", Encyclopaedia of Islam, 2nd ed., vol. 3.
  6. Quran 112; John 1:1, 1:14.
